headline: Overcapacity becomes a four-economy industrial-policy test
dek: Washington is preparing action on excess production, while China, Japan, and South Korea face different degrees of exposure.
story_title: From China’s factories to America’s tariffs: who bears the cost of excess capacity?
story_html:
United States: Washington is preparing to release the findings of an investigation into foreign industrial overcapacity within weeks. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the United States would not quietly absorb goods produced in excess, signalling that tariffs or other trade measures remain possible. The probe is aimed primarily at China, but its scope is broader: Washington is also examining whether production models in Japan and South Korea distort competition. The policy challenge is to protect domestic manufacturers without raising costs for American consumers or provoking retaliation. ([en.sedaily.com](https://en.sedaily.com/international/2026/10/02/us-vows-action-on-overcapacity-within-weeks?utm_source=openai))

China: China is the central target because its manufacturing system has expanded capacity rapidly in industries such as electric vehicles, batteries, solar equipment, and other strategic goods. From Beijing’s perspective, large-scale production supports technological upgrading and export competitiveness. From Washington’s perspective, however, subsidised finance, weak domestic demand, and aggressive exports can create a global glut. That disagreement matters beyond the bilateral relationship: if the United States imposes new duties, Chinese producers may redirect more shipments toward other markets, intensifying competitive pressure across Asia. ([en.sedaily.com](https://en.sedaily.com/international/2026/10/02/us-vows-action-on-overcapacity-within-weeks?utm_source=openai))

Japan: Japan is not being treated simply as a victim of Chinese competition. Greer criticised Tokyo for allegedly keeping “zombie firms” alive—companies that remain in business despite weak productivity or poor profitability. Such firms can preserve excess capacity and delay industrial restructuring. The accusation is politically sensitive because Japan’s policymakers are trying to strengthen domestic supply chains while avoiding a return to deflation. Tokyo therefore faces a delicate balancing act: support strategic industries, but do not protect inefficient companies indefinitely. ([en.sedaily.com](https://en.sedaily.com/international/2026/10/02/us-vows-action-on-overcapacity-within-weeks?utm_source=openai))

South Korea: South Korea is also included in the U.S. investigation, creating uncertainty for an economy heavily dependent on exports and manufacturing. Korean semiconductor and technology shares were unsettled in early Asian trading, while September inflation remained above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target. Seoul must defend its exporters while preserving the benefits of its trade relationship with Washington. The Korea-U.S. trade agreement may limit any new tariff burden, but it cannot remove the strategic risk altogether. ([mrjjxw.com](https://www.mrjjxw.com/articles/2026-10-02/4596643.html?utm_source=openai))

The shared theme is not that all four economies suffer from the same problem. Rather, overcapacity has become a test of how governments define fair competition. The United States is preparing to police foreign production; China is defending an export-led industrial model; Japan is being pressed to restructure weak firms; and South Korea is trying to avoid collateral damage. The immediate question is whether trade barriers will produce healthier competition—or merely shift surplus goods and political pressure from one market to another.
b2_summary: The United States may take action against foreign overcapacity, especially from China, within weeks. Washington says excess production can damage American manufacturers and workers. China sees large-scale manufacturing as a way to improve technology and exports, but other countries worry about a global glut. Japan faces criticism for supporting weak companies, while South Korea is included in the U.S. investigation because of its manufacturing strength. These economies do not have identical problems, but they are connected by a growing debate about subsidies, excess supply, tariffs, and industrial policy.

concept.title: What is overcapacity?
concept.explanation: Overcapacity means a country or industry can produce more goods than customers currently want to buy. Factories may continue producing because governments provide subsidies or cheap loans. The result can be lower prices, weaker profits, trade disputes, and tariffs from countries that believe their own producers are being harmed.

quiz.question: Why is South Korea concerned about the U.S. overcapacity investigation?
options: Because Korea has stopped exporting manufactured goods
Because Korean exporters could face trade pressure despite not being the main target
Because the Bank of Korea has already imposed new tariffs
quiz.explanation: South Korea is included in the investigation and depends heavily on manufacturing exports, so it could face pressure even though China is the main target.

one_sentence: The overcapacity debate is no longer only about China; it is becoming a test of how all four economies balance industrial ambition, market discipline, and trade diplomacy.
